27	## Duels at sea (§6, §14)
28	
29	- **Encounters in the room.** Each world step (20 Hz), after sailing, `MatchRoom` builds one tick's snapshot for `stepEncounters` (`docs/encounters.md`): every ship's position and heading, whether its player is connected, pressed J since the last world step (the input gate latches it like E), has a loaded arena, or started a collection or cache claim last tick (which ends protection). It passes back the reports of duels that ended since the last tick, and a settlement only once the ledger has settled the duel (below). It applies the events: `duel-reserved` stops both ships and opens a duel; `duel-started` starts its fight; a ready-check `duel-forfeited` or `duel-cancelled` ends it; `player-returned` and `player-respawned` move a ship (at rest, or moored at the dock). Everything else (attempts, protection, cooldowns, the loser's wait) is mirrored from the rules' state. The rules alone choose targets and decide hits, returns and docks; the room never re-implements them. Reserved and respawning ships get neutral input, so they stay put. The rules run from control start, when every ship gets the departure's protection, to the match's end.
30	- **One duel machine.** `DuelMachine` (`apps/server/src/duelMachine.ts`) is the duel both rooms run: seats and their `DuelInputGate`s, the 180-frame countdown with round-trip probes and the input delay chosen 30 frames before its end, `DuelAuthority` stepped at 60 Hz with a bundle every third frame, the reconnection bookkeeping (a dropped seat is marked away, a returning one gets a snapshot bundle) and the forfeits decided together at the next frame boundary. It writes a lobby schema and sends through a callback, so the host room owns clients and timers. `DuelRoom` starts the fight when the countdown ends (`start: "countdown"`); the match room starts it when the rules say so (`start: "called"`: the countdown is over and both fighters sent `duel-ready`). A countdown that ends with a fighter still loading waits in `waiting`, without probes; clients drop their session then, so the fight's clock starts from the fight's own frames. The match room keeps each duel's lobby for 2 s after settlement (`DUEL_RESULT_TICKS`), so both read the result.
31	- **Absence** (§12, on the world tick). A drop anywhere disconnects the player in the ledger at once; the ship stays in the world, grapplable, for the 60 s seat reservation. A fighter away from an unfinished duel for 10 s, counted in world ticks, forfeits it (both on one frame: no winner, reported as cancelled) and respawns as any loser, keeping the seat. Back before the deadline, the same player continues (`reconnectPlayer`; a fighter gets a snapshot bundle). Colyseus' `allowReconnection` is only an outer bound (70 s) that keeps the socket's slot: at the ledger's deadline the room expires the reservation and releases that slot; any other leave (consented, or the outer bound first) is a quit.
32	- **Message routing.** A duel's `duel-frames` and `duel-probe` go to its two fighters only, with `client.send`; the room routes `duel-input`, `duel-probe` echoes and `duel-ready` from a session to that session's duel and drops them from anyone else. In the browser, `SeaDuelRouter` listens for the duel messages once per match and hands them to the duel client of the moment (a message that beats the lobby's patch waits for it); the same `DuelClient` runs a standalone duel over `duelRoomTransport`.
33	- **Visibility (§16).** The state's new maps are filtered per client like `ships`: `grapples` (telegraphs, keyed by attacker: in a view when its attacker is in sight, or when it is the viewer's own or aimed at the viewer; each attempt has a twin entry with `defenderId` blank, which a viewer who sees the attacker but not the target gets instead), `markers` (a duel's position and reservation tick under an opaque key, nothing naming its fighters: in a view within the sight radius), `caches` (a recovery cache's position and dock, no contents: within the sight radius), `status` (a player's own mode, protection, cooldown, respawn tick, gold, rubbings, holds and theft choice: only the player's), `duels` (a duel's lobby: only its two fighters'). A ship in a duel or waiting to respawn is in no one else's view; its own player keeps it until it waits to respawn. A fighter or a player waiting to respawn sees no other ship, telegraph, marker or cache. Integration tests check the decoded state and the raw frames of a watcher in sight and a stranger out of it.
34	- **One game per page.** The match page's Phaser game (canvas renderer, see Rendering) holds the sea scene and the arena scene (`MatchGame`); a duel puts the sea to sleep and starts the arena with that duel's client, and its end wakes the sea (`data-scene` says which shows). The duel HUD moves beside the canvas meanwhile. The standalone duel page's game holds only the arena. The helm is read during a duel (so a J tapped in the arena is not kept) but the sea gets neutral input.

36	## Rubbings in the room (§4, §11, §12, `rubbings-theft`)
37	
38	- **The ledger per match.** `MatchRoom` creates a `slice` ledger with the match, seeded with the ledger's seed derived from the match's master secret (below). Its sources stand at each regular island's docks (two per island, in dock id order), all locked at the start behind their island's ruin (below). The ledger is the only writer of rubbings and gold: the room calls its operations and never moves either itself, and after every world tick it checks `checkLedger` and its own invariant (every player the ledger counts in the match has a ship, and every ship such a player) in development and tests.
39	- **Collecting and claiming.** Holding E moored at a dock is one gesture: E moors, and the same hold works on E's target there, the island's first sealed source of a type the player lacks, else a cached rubbing of a type they lack (fixed type order). The room continues the ledger's hold every held tick; releasing E, casting off, a reservation or a disconnect cancels it, and progress resets. Starting a hold ends protection on the next tick.
40	- **Settlement order.** Each world tick: `advanceLedger` (a closed choice window settles with the default); the §12 timers (duel absence, seat expiry into a cache at the respawn dock); `stepEncounters`, whose reports tell the ledger a fight's result and the rules its end, and tell the rules `settled` only once the ledger has settled the duel; then the holds. On a win with an eligible type the winner gets 5 s to send `choose-theft`; a draw, a cancellation or a win with nothing to take settles at once (gold still moves on a win). Only then do the players return. The fighters' lobby stays in their views through the choice. Both fighters' notices carry the settlement's tick, who picked the stolen type (`settledChoice`: the winner, or the default at the deadline) and the choice's deadline tick, so the purse says "You chose Moon" (the loser: "They chose Moon") or "Taken by default: Moon". The web client maps a key (1, 2) or a click on option *n* to a type in one pure function (`chosenTheftType`, `hud.ts`) before it sends `choose-theft`.
41	- **Messages.** `choose-theft` `{ duel, type }` (protocol v6): the opaque key of the sender's own duel lobby and a rubbing type, zod-validated, at most 64 bytes and 8 a second; the ledger accepts it only from the winner, inside the window, for an eligible type, and otherwise changes nothing. Collecting and claiming need no message: E is the input's interact button.
42	- **What each client sees (§16).** Gold, rubbings, the hold and its progress, the last results and the theft options are in the player's own `status` entry only. The island's sealed types and a cache's contents are filled in only while the player is moored at that island's dock or that cache's dock. A cache is a contentless marker at its dock, in a view within the sight radius. Integration tests check raw frames: an onlooker in sight of a collection and a duel never receives a rubbing type at all.
43	- **Leaving.** A reservation that expires removes the player and puts their remaining rubbings in one cache at the dock the encounter rules would respawn them at; a quit (or Colyseus' outer bound) forfeits a duel in progress and caches the rest at the dock nearest the ship by sea (`seaPathCosts`). No path removes a ship while the ledger still counts its player. A cache never despawns; claimed empty, it disappears.

45	## The match: lobby to results (§2, §5, `match-online`)
46	
47	- **Lobby.** A private match opens in its lobby (`phase` in the synced state). Its players are listed by seat ("Player 2": join order from 1; the state names players by seat, never by session id, so a ship's id still first reaches a client when it comes into sight, §16). The first joiner hosts (the host passes on when they leave). The host's `start-match` (zod-validated, empty, 4 a second) goes to the match module's `stepMatch`, which starts the ready countdown with 2 or more players present (`PRIVATE_MIN_PLAYERS`, the single source: the content's `privateMatch.minPlayers` of 1 is stale and not read) and otherwise answers `start-refused` (`too-few`, `not-host`). From the countdown on, the listing's metadata says `started` and admission refuses every join with "That match has already started" (the room's `onJoin` refuses too); if the countdown falls back to the lobby (fewer than 2 left), joins reopen. Ships are held (neutral input) until control starts and again after the end.
48	- **Ready and departure.** The countdown lasts `readyTicks` (20 s) while clients preload (the arena scene is already in the page's one game). The flow's `control-started` tick starts everything that counts from it: the encounter rules' state with every ship protected for `spawnProtectionTicks` (45 s, which is also the departure's length), the claim config (`createClaimConfig`, its `deadlineTick` = control start + `deadlineTicks`), and the intel config and state. The timer the HUD shows is the match module's `remaining`, whose duration is the claim rules' `deadlineTicks`: both configs are built from one set of rules (`matchConfigFor`, `claimConfigFor` in `matchFlow.ts`), and a unit test and an integration test hold them equal.
49	- **Tick order** (each world tick while the match runs): `advanceLedger` (closed theft windows), the §12 timers, then §5's order: **encounters** (accepted reservations first) → the ledger's holds → **claim** channel (`stepClaim`: every ship with `holdsAllTypes` from the ledger, E, speed, connection, protection, and the encounter rules' reserved duels) → **match flow** (`stepMatch`: the joins, leaves and starts since the last tick, this tick's accomplishments, and the claim's `match-ended`) → **intel reveals** (`stepIntel`). Before control start only the timers and the flow run. The room drops reports naming a player the flow does not know before calling `stepMatch`, which throws on them: one pure function over plain data (`knownFlowReports`, `apps/server/src/flowReports.ts`) drops a duel's end naming an unknown fighter, a claim's end naming an unknown winner and any accomplishment naming an unknown player, and keeps joins (known from then on), leaves, starts and a fault. The room handles no `join-refused`: it reports a join only in the lobby (its `onJoin` refuses one after it), a lobby step applies joins before any start, and the room seats no more players than the flow has seats.
50	- **Reveals.** The intel module reads the ledger's rubbings and the ships each tick; the room delivers only its reveal messages (rumors and the journal come with `intel-online`), each to exactly its recipients as `reveal` messages: `final-sector` to everyone at the first full set (also kept in the public state, name and index only), `final-route` with the exact claim point only to a full-set holder (also in that player's own status, with `routeActive`), `final-route-inactive` to a holder who lost a type, `sector-reveal` at minute 20 and `carrier-report` from minute 28 to everyone. An integration test checks raw frames: the other player never receives a `final-route`. The browser shows each as a banner and in a list; the holder gets a compass line, an arrow off the ship, the treasure circle and a minimap mark. In play everyone else's compass shows, inactive, "No treasure route yet". The page's decisions are pure view models, unit-tested branch by branch: `flowView` (`flowHud.ts`: each flow element's text, state and visibility) and `treasureView` (`treasureView.ts`: the sea scene's circle, marks, arrow and claim rings as shapes); `applyFlow` and the scene's `drawTreasure` only copy them into the page and the canvas.
51	- **The claim.** Stopped inside the treasure circle, holding every type and E, unreserved: the claim module's channel runs for `channelTicks` (10 s); starting it ends protection (the encounter rules hear it on the next tick). The player's status carries the channel's progress and the last reset's reason (moved, released, a duel, a lost type, a disconnect); the claim panel shows them with "Any rival in range can interrupt you with a grapple". The room can't produce a lost-type reset (`ineligible`) in a running channel: a player loses a type only through a duel's theft, and that duel's reservation resets the channel (`duel`) on the tick it's accepted, long before the settlement moves the rubbing. The claim module's own tests cover that branch, and the claim panel's unit test shows its text. Ships channelling show it to whoever sees them (a gold ring), and those players are warned. On `match-ended` the flow ends the match: outcomes freeze (a running duel is cancelled without theft, no ship takes input, nothing more is stepped).
52	- **Endings and results.** `claim` (a winner), `deadline` (no winner; a claim completing on the deadline tick wins), `abandoned` (everyone left after the lobby; stepped once more as the room closes) and `aborted` (a world tick that throws is caught as §12's server fault). The accomplishments come from the ledger (`docs/objectives.md`) and settled duels: a rubbing leaving a source is collected, one leaving a cache is a cache claimed, one moving between players is a theft and a loss, one going into a cache is a loss; a settled win or draw counts for both fighters, a cancelled duel for neither. The results (the flow's) are synced to everyone once, shown until players leave (Back to lobby returns to the landing page), and recorded in the process's outcome list (`recordedOutcomes`).
53	- **Seeds.** One private master secret per match (32 bytes of `node:crypto`'s `randomBytes`). Each system's seed is `HMAC-SHA-256(secret, "pirate-sea-race/seed/v1/" + system)`, its first four bytes: `world`, `ledger`, `final-socket`, `intel`, `ruins`, `fruit` (the fruit deal), and each duel's `duel:<n>`. No raw seed feeds two systems and none reads the match code; unit and integration tests check both.
54	- **Test hooks** (`MatchTuning.testHooks`, off by default, never set by an entry point): `injectFault()` makes the next world tick throw (an `aborted` ending), `pauseAfterTick(tick)` / `resumeWorld()` stop the clock after a tick so a test lines an input up with an exact tick (a grapple landing on a claim's completion tick, a claim completing on the deadline tick), and `injectFlowReports(reports)` adds reports to the flow's next step (a ghost player's, to show they are dropped).
55	- **Coverage.** `docs/match-online-coverage.md` lists every room-level and UI branch this feature added or changed, each with the test that fails without it. `recordedOutcomes` keeps only the latest 64 (`outcomes.ts`).

74	## The duel (combat spike)
75	
76	- **Duel room.** `DuelRoom` (room name `duel`) holds one duel, a `DuelMachine`: two players, or one in practice against a server-side dummy (player two, `idle` or `guard`). It is admitted like a match, by the same code in `admission.ts`: a one-time create token, `onAuth` before any seat, the room's own check, `filterBy(['code', 'createToken'])`, no token in the listing. The countdown (180 frames) starts once every seat is taken; the machine probes round trips during it, chooses the shared input delay 30 frames before the end, then steps `DuelAuthority` at 60 Hz, which the room's `setFixedTimestep` drives. Inputs go through `DuelInputGate`, which admits them through the same `InputAdmission` as the world's `InputGate` (the rate window and the protocol validation: 128 bytes, 60 a second of room ticks, increasing sequence, 30 frames of lead), so the two cannot drift, and counts its drops. Frame bundles and probes are Colyseus messages; the lobby is a small Schema state. A drop keeps the seat for 10 s (`allowReconnection`); leaving, or staying away, forfeits, decided at the next frame boundary (two forfeits on one frame: no winner). The rules and rates are in `docs/duel.md`.
77	- **One rollback core.** The browser's `DuelClient` and `HeadlessDuelClient` both run `DuelClientSession` from `@pirate-sea-race/simulation/netcode`; they differ only in transport and input (keyboard or script), and each plays over a duel room or a match room. The arena draws the predicted state; the HUD shows the confirmed one (server-equal health, stamina and clock) and the room's result. `window.__duel` exposes the session's counters and tagged inputs, read-only, for the browser tests.
78	- **Impairment harness.** `ImpairmentProxy` is a TCP proxy (Node's `net`, no new dependency) between a client and the server. It forwards HTTP untouched in content and splits the WebSocket stream into frames; each frame waits half the round trip plus a uniform ±jitter/2 in its direction, never overtaking the frame before it, and a lost frame (seeded draw) waits a further retransmission timeout (200 ms), stalling everything behind it as TCP does. `sever()` cuts every connection (optionally refusing new ones) for the reconnect tests. `tests/integration/duelHarness.test.ts` runs a scripted duel between two headless clients through it, with no impairment and at 80 ms, 20 ms jitter and 1 % loss (and `seaDuelHarness.test.ts` the same duel at sea, at 80 ms, 20 ms and 1 %, with the scripts and budget of `harness.ts`), and requires no desync at any of the ~180 hash checks per client, no rate-limited input, and corrections at most one per change of the opponent's applied input plus one per own substituted input, and at most 8 a second; it prints and annotates the counts. `replayRecordedDuel` replays a log (for example the pairs a client received) with `replayDuel`.
79	- **Dev latency.** Only in `npm run dev` (`import.meta.env.DEV`), `?rtt=80&jitter=20` on the page delays that browser's duel socket both ways, probes and pings included; the build smoke test checks the production bundle does not contain it. The browser checks run the production build, so the setting is tested below the browser: `apps/web/src/devLatency.ts` has no DOM dependency, unit tests with fake timers check its delay, jitter bound and order on a real SDK room, and `tests/integration/devLatency.test.ts` wraps two headless duel clients in it and checks that the room's measured round trip and chosen input delay rise above the same duel without it.

81	## Rules the code keeps
82	
83	- **Purity.** `simulation`, `protocol` and `content` import no Phaser, Colyseus, DOM, timers, wall-clock time or `Math.random`, and call no floating-point transcendental `Math` function. Their tsconfig leaves out the DOM library, and `tests/unit/purity.test.ts` fails on a violation.
84	- **Integers.** Every number in the simulation state is an integer, so `hashState` (64-bit FNV-1a over a canonical serialization) does not depend on the JavaScript engine; a determinism test replays an input log.
85	- **One clock.** The room steps the simulation 60 times a second with Colyseus `setFixedTimestep`. World logic runs on frames divisible by 3 (20 Hz); the room then mirrors the plain state into its Schema and updates the views, and Colyseus patches clients at 20 Hz. Integration tests measure both rates, also with eight sailing ships in one cluster.
86	- **The server alone writes state.** At sea, clients send only `input` messages, `{seq, frame, buttons, moveX, moveY}`, validated with zod (the grapple is a button: the rules choose its target, never the client). `InputGate` drops, and counts, messages over the rate cap (60 per second of match time) or over 128 bytes, malformed ones (axes outside [-1, 1] are rejected, not clamped), ones whose sequence number is not higher than the last, and ones tagged more than 30 frames ahead. A held input lapses to neutral after 15 frames. An accepted world input applies from the server's next step whatever frame it names, since sea clients do not predict; a duel input applies to exactly the frame it names (`docs/duel.md`). Unknown message types are dropped. Colyseus's own limits sit above these: WebSocket frames over 4 KiB and more than 240 messages a second disconnect.
87	- **Joining.** Matches and duels share the admission code (`apps/server/src/admission.ts`). Colyseus serves `create`, `join`, `joinOrCreate` and `joinById` over HTTP and reserves a seat before any room check, so a private match is guarded in three layers. The static `onAuth` runs before any seat is reserved: it refuses a mismatched protocol version (426), a request with neither or both of `code` and `createToken` or a malformed token (400), an unknown code (404) and a full match (409). A `create` carries a one-time 128-bit `createToken`; the room is registered with `filterBy(['code', 'createToken'])` and `onCreate` replaces the listing's metadata with `{code, custom}`, so no listing holds a token and a token-carrying request can only create. The room's `onJoin` is the backstop, and the only check `joinById` meets after `onAuth`: one seat with the creator's token, then only seats with the match's code (404 for another code, 403 otherwise). Refusal messages stay under 100 bytes. A caller who knows a room id can still hold seats with `joinById` until each reservation expires (15 s).
88	- **Rendering.** The client draws the ships the server sent 100 ms in the past, interpolating between patches; the HUD lists their latest decoded state. The camera follows the player's ship over a Phaser tile map at 24 px a tile (the 480 px sight circle fits the 800 × 560 view) that leaves open sea to the background colour, keeping a software renderer fast. The sea does not predict; the duel arena does (above). Both of the page's Phaser games use the canvas renderer: the standalone duel page's arena, and the match page's one game holding the sea and the arena. With `Phaser.AUTO`, headless Chromium (the GPU-less case: WebGL in software, on the main thread) starved the duel client's 4 ms tick during a fight at sea: the `sea-duel` browser test, which records the `DuelClient`'s tick intervals through the fight and requires their 95th percentile under 16 ms, measured 135 ms. With `Phaser.CANVAS` it measured 8.5 ms (host) and 8.9 ms (guest), so the match game now uses the canvas renderer too.
89	
90	## Toolchain
91	
92	npm workspaces, TypeScript 7.0.2 (`tsc` for typechecks and package builds), Vite 8.3.0 (web build), Vitest 5.0.1 (`unit` and `integration` projects), tsx (map script and dev server), Phaser 4.2.1, `colyseus` 0.18.8 with `@colyseus/schema` 5.0.34, `@colyseus/sdk` 0.18.4, zod 4.6.5, Playwright 1.63.0. Workspace packages export a `@pirate-sea-race/source` condition that points at `src/`, so development and tests need no build. `npm run build` compiles each package to `dist/` in dependency order, then `scripts/smoke-build.ts` loads every workspace export from `dist/`, starts the built server on a free port, creates a match through the SDK, waits for the creator's ship and checks that no test-placement route answers, with every wait bounded. `colyseus` brings `uWebSockets.js` in from GitHub, so `npm ci` needs github.com as well as the npm registry. The duel added no dependency: `packages/test-tools` now also depends on the workspace's `@pirate-sea-race/simulation`, and the smoke test also loads `@pirate-sea-race/simulation/netcode` from `dist/`, checks the web bundle for the dev-only latency setting, and plays the first frames of a practice duel on the built server.
93

# Architecture

The §14 browser architecture as far as the §3 sea, the §6 encounters at sea, §18 stage 2's whole winnable match (a lobby, the collect, fight, steal and recover loop, the reveals, the claim and the results), and the §18 combat spike: browsers gather in a private match's lobby on one authoritative Colyseus room, the shared fixed-step simulation sails the ships over an authored tile map, and every browser draws what the server lets it see. A grapple that lands starts a 1v1 duel inside that room, fought with §15's prediction and rollback (the netcode is in `docs/duel.md`); the same duel also runs in a standalone duel room, for practice and private 1v1s. The objective ledger (`docs/objectives.md`) runs inside the room and is the only writer of rubbings and gold.

| Workspace | §14 component | What it holds now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `apps/web` | Browser client and web shell | Landing page, the lobby panel (code, players, the host's Start), the clock bar (phase, 35:00 timer, the final sector), reveal banners, the compass and the claim panel with its risk line, the results screen (`flowHud.ts`), HUD (with the island's types, the cache's contents and the hold's progress while moored), the purse beside the game (gold, rubbings, the last settlement, the winner's theft choice on keys 1 and 2), the ruin panel (R) and the fruit panel (F) with the HUD's kit line, keyboard helm (E and J latched), input sender, snapshot interpolation, one Phaser game per page: the sea scene (tile map, following camera, ships, telegraphs, duel markers, cache chests, fogged minimap) and the arena scene; the duel client over a transport seam (keyboard with tap latch, `DuelClientSession` loop, duel HUD, dev-only latency setting) |
| `apps/server` | Match process | `MatchRoom` (one Colyseus room per match: the match flow, the simulation, the encounter rules, its duels at sea, the objective ledger, the claim and the reveals), the flow configs built from one set of rules (`matchFlow.ts`), the per-system seeds (`matchSeeds.ts`), the ledger's place on the sea (`objectives.ts`: source sites, E's target, the nearest dock by sea), the ruins' and the fruit pedestals' places (`ruins.ts`, `fruits.ts`), the Schema mirror, per-client views, input gate, entry points; `DuelRoom`; `DuelMachine`, the duel both rooms run, and its input gate; the shared private admission |
| `packages/simulation` | Shared fixed-step functions | Integer match state, heading table, sailing, collisions, docking, stopping and returning ships, visibility rule, seeded generator, `hashState`; the encounter rules (`/encounters`, `docs/encounters.md`); the duel (`/duel`) and its netcode (`/netcode`: `DuelAuthority`, `DuelRollback`, `DuelClock`, `DuelClientSession`, the input-delay policy) |
| `packages/protocol` | Data contracts (§16) | Protocol version (9: the fruit), create and join options, the input schemas and validation (buttons: interact, grapple, fruit), the fruit inspection and duel kits, the duel messages (with `duel-ready` at sea), the theft choice (`choose-theft`), the lobby's `start-match` and `start-refused`, the `reveal` messages, refusal messages, the test-only placement request, source layout, timings and final-socket secret |
| `packages/content` | Content and tuning (§17) | The slice sea (generated from Tiled), the Tiled converter, map validators, ship tuning, sight and engagement ranges, rules presets, frame budgets |
| `packages/test-tools` | Test harness (§17) | `HeadlessClient`: a browserless player on the real Colyseus SDK that also records the raw frames and reveals it receives, starts a match from the lobby, reads its route, claim and results, and fights at sea through its `fighter`; `HeadlessDuelClient` (the browser's `DuelClientSession` on the SDK, driven by a script, over a duel room or a match room), `ImpairmentProxy`, and `replayRecordedDuel` |

The HTTP service, PostgreSQL, static hosting and monitoring are not built yet (`infra/` is a placeholder).

## The sea

- **Map format and pipeline.** The map is `assets/source/maps/slice-sea.tmj`, in a documented subset of Tiled's JSON format (`packages/content/src/tiledMap.ts`): orthogonal, finite, 24 px tiles (`TILE_PIXELS`, as drawn); one imageless tileset whose tiles carry a `type` of `sea`, `land`, `shoal` or `dock`; a `terrain` layer as a plain gid array; an `objects` layer with a named `island` rectangle per island (property `theme`), a `spawn` point per slot (properties `slot` and `facing`), one `hub` point and a `final-socket` rectangle per hidden final-island socket (properties `claimX`, `claimY`). Nothing else is accepted. `npm run map:build -- --from-sketch` writes it from one mirrored ASCII quarter (`sliceSeaSketch.ts`; a unit test fails when they differ). `npm run map:build` (`scripts/build-map.ts`) converts it into `packages/content/src/maps/sliceSea.ts` (terrain rows and objects) if it passes the validators; a unit test fails when that module is stale (it reads the `.tmj` as a Vite `?raw` import).
- **Validators.** `validateSeaMap` checks §2 and §3: four small islands, each land tile inside one island rectangle, each island with a dock beside its land and open sea; shoals; eight spawn slots on open sea outside the islands' bounding box and pairwise beyond `ENGAGEMENT_RANGE_TILES` (6); every dock and slot reachable by sea; and, by eight-way shortest paths (no cut corners) at full speed: each island's nearest neighbour 20–40 s away, no dock-or-slot crossing over 90 s, a dock within 40 s of every slot. No empty stretches: every navigable tile is within the sight radius of land, a shoal or a dock (not the edge). Routes meet: closing the disc around the hub (open sea near the centre; radius half the sight radius, so ships in it see each other) lengthens or cuts every shortest path between docks of different islands. At most 112 tiles a side. The slice sea (111 × 111 tiles, midline shoal walls open only in the hub's disc): neighbours 26 s apart, longest crossing 39 s, water within 9.9 tiles of an obstacle, 90 % open sea.
- **Final-island sockets (§3, §5).** `map.finalSockets` holds four identical dockless islets (one sketched islet, mirrored), each a rectangle of at most 6 × 6 and a claim tile: open sea beside it whose centre is the claim point, the treasure circle's centre (`TREASURE_CIRCLE_RADIUS_TILES`). Their land belongs to no island, so docks, sailing, respawn and visibility treat them as plain land. `validateFinalSockets` (run by `validateSeaMap`) requires every claim tile within 90 s of every spawn slot, at least two sockets in any sector holding one (`sectorOf`: column ⌊3x / width⌋, row ⌊3y / height⌋, the grid a sector reveal must use), at least 12 navigable tiles in each circle, and nothing within 8 tiles of what the running tests sail on (`keepClearZones`: the hub, spawn slots, docks and 14 tiles out from each, the out-of-sight row). The slice's sockets sit two in the north-centre sector and two in the south-centre one. `chooseFinalSocket(map, secret)` picks a match's socket from a 32-bit secret, mixed by the murmur3 finaliser before the modulo; the room passes the final-socket seed derived from its master secret (below), never the public match seed (§3).
- **Sailing.** Positions are integer sub-units (256 a tile); headings are 64 directions, 0 east, clockwise (y grows down), unit vectors from a literal cosine table. Each world step the throttle (`-moveY`) accelerates towards 39 sub-units a step (3.05 tiles a second), brakes, or reverses slowly from a stop; `moveX` turns a heading a step (3.2 s a circle); none coasts to a stop. On 24 px tiles that handles like the old five tiles a second on 16 px (unit tests hold it within 25 %). The hull is a square of half-size 80. A move sweeps each axis in turn through the tile columns or rows its leading edge enters and stops flush at the first land, shoal or map edge: a ship slides along an obstacle met at an angle, runs aground head-on, and never tunnels.
- **Docking.** Hold E near a dock to moor, at any speed and throttle: with the hull on or beside the berth tile (unless pinched), or within reach with a clear run, it moves to the dock's centre, stops and records the dock, so no arrival slides past or grounds beside it (pinched: a diagonal tile whose two shared tiles are blocked). It stays moored while E or the throttle it moored with (`mooredThrottle`) is held; pressing a throttle after releasing that one, or the other direction, casts off. An input stall does not: the server gives a lapsed client no input, keeping the latch. The keyboard keeps a tap of E until its next read (not past a blur), the server until its next step; then the HUD says "Press E to dock".
- **Visibility boundary (§16).** The room's `ships` map is tagged `.view()`. Each client gets a `StateView`; after every mirror the room puts into it the client's own ship and each ship within `SIGHT_RADIUS_TILES` (10, `visibleShipIds`) and takes out the rest, so Colyseus encodes no other ship into that client's patches (an integration test checks the decoded state and the raw frames). `players` in the state is the public player count. Terrain is static content every client bundles, never synced; the minimap fog is client-side presentation, not a security boundary.
- **Test placement.** Tests place ships through `POST /__test/place` (code, session id, tile, heading); its tile bounds come from the map. Only the dev and test entry (`apps/server/src/dev.ts`) offers it, when `PIRATE_SEA_RACE_TEST_PLACEMENT=1`; the production entry (`main.ts`) never reads that, which the build smoke test checks. It only moves a ship: admission and views are unchanged.
- **Test-only timings and source layout.** `startGameServer({ matchTuning })` gives every match of that server other rules (a short seat reservation, respawn wait, duel absence, ready countdown, protection, match, channel or reveals), a pinned source layout, a pinned final-socket secret, an injected master secret, or the room's test hooks; integration tests use it and assert in world ticks. Colyseus has one matchmaker per process, so each integration test file has one set of timings. The dev and test entry also reads `PIRATE_SEA_RACE_TEST_SOURCES` (for example `sun,sun|moon,moon|sun,sun|moon,moon`: the types of each island's sources), `PIRATE_SEA_RACE_TEST_TIMINGS` (for example `ready=60,protection=20,match=12000`, in world ticks; also `sectors` and `carriers`) and `PIRATE_SEA_RACE_TEST_FINAL_SECRET` (a 32-bit secret), which the browser tests set so a scenario picks an island by type, plays a whole match in a minute and knows where the treasure is. With the test placement setting, `POST /__test/next-match-timings` (the same timing names, as JSON) gives only the next match created its own timings, so the `match-deadline` scenario runs a 20 s match. All are off by default. `main.ts` reads none (the build smoke test starts it with all of them set, malformed, and checks the 20 s countdown and 35:00 timer) and turns the per-tick invariant checks off.

## Duels at sea (§6, §14)

- **Encounters in the room.** Each world step (20 Hz), after sailing, `MatchRoom` builds one tick's snapshot for `stepEncounters` (`docs/encounters.md`): every ship's position and heading, whether its player is connected, pressed J since the last world step (the input gate latches it like E), has a loaded arena, or started a collection or cache claim last tick (which ends protection). It passes back the reports of duels that ended since the last tick, and a settlement only once the ledger has settled the duel (below). It applies the events: `duel-reserved` stops both ships and opens a duel; `duel-started` starts its fight; a ready-check `duel-forfeited` or `duel-cancelled` ends it; `player-returned` and `player-respawned` move a ship (at rest, or moored at the dock). Everything else (attempts, protection, cooldowns, the loser's wait) is mirrored from the rules' state. The rules alone choose targets and decide hits, returns and docks; the room never re-implements them. Reserved and respawning ships get neutral input, so they stay put. The rules run from control start, when every ship gets the departure's protection, to the match's end.
- **One duel machine.** `DuelMachine` (`apps/server/src/duelMachine.ts`) is the duel both rooms run: seats and their `DuelInputGate`s, the 180-frame countdown with round-trip probes and the input delay chosen 30 frames before its end, `DuelAuthority` stepped at 60 Hz with a bundle every third frame, the reconnection bookkeeping (a dropped seat is marked away, a returning one gets a snapshot bundle) and the forfeits decided together at the next frame boundary. It writes a lobby schema and sends through a callback, so the host room owns clients and timers. `DuelRoom` starts the fight when the countdown ends (`start: "countdown"`); the match room starts it when the rules say so (`start: "called"`: the countdown is over and both fighters sent `duel-ready`). A countdown that ends with a fighter still loading waits in `waiting`, without probes; clients drop their session then, so the fight's clock starts from the fight's own frames. The match room keeps each duel's lobby for 2 s after settlement (`DUEL_RESULT_TICKS`), so both read the result.
- **Absence** (§12, on the world tick). A drop anywhere disconnects the player in the ledger at once; the ship stays in the world, grapplable, for the 60 s seat reservation. A fighter away from an unfinished duel for 10 s, counted in world ticks, forfeits it (both on one frame: no winner, reported as cancelled) and respawns as any loser, keeping the seat. Back before the deadline, the same player continues (`reconnectPlayer`; a fighter gets a snapshot bundle). Colyseus' `allowReconnection` is only an outer bound (70 s) that keeps the socket's slot: at the ledger's deadline the room expires the reservation and releases that slot; any other leave (consented, or the outer bound first) is a quit.
- **Message routing.** A duel's `duel-frames` and `duel-probe` go to its two fighters only, with `client.send`; the room routes `duel-input`, `duel-probe` echoes and `duel-ready` from a session to that session's duel and drops them from anyone else. In the browser, `SeaDuelRouter` listens for the duel messages once per match and hands them to the duel client of the moment (a message that beats the lobby's patch waits for it); the same `DuelClient` runs a standalone duel over `duelRoomTransport`.
- **Visibility (§16).** The state's new maps are filtered per client like `ships`: `grapples` (telegraphs, keyed by attacker: in a view when its attacker is in sight, or when it is the viewer's own or aimed at the viewer; each attempt has a twin entry with `defenderId` blank, which a viewer who sees the attacker but not the target gets instead), `markers` (a duel's position and reservation tick under an opaque key, nothing naming its fighters: in a view within the sight radius), `caches` (a recovery cache's position and dock, no contents: within the sight radius), `status` (a player's own mode, protection, cooldown, respawn tick, gold, rubbings, holds and theft choice: only the player's), `duels` (a duel's lobby: only its two fighters'). A ship in a duel or waiting to respawn is in no one else's view; its own player keeps it until it waits to respawn. A fighter or a player waiting to respawn sees no other ship, telegraph, marker or cache. Integration tests check the decoded state and the raw frames of a watcher in sight and a stranger out of it.
- **One game per page.** The match page's Phaser game (canvas renderer, see Rendering) holds the sea scene and the arena scene (`MatchGame`); a duel puts the sea to sleep and starts the arena with that duel's client, and its end wakes the sea (`data-scene` says which shows). The duel HUD moves beside the canvas meanwhile. The standalone duel page's game holds only the arena. The helm is read during a duel (so a J tapped in the arena is not kept) but the sea gets neutral input.

## Rubbings in the room (§4, §11, §12, `rubbings-theft`)

- **The ledger per match.** `MatchRoom` creates a `slice` ledger with the match, seeded with the ledger's seed derived from the match's master secret (below). Its sources stand at each regular island's docks (two per island, in dock id order), all locked at the start behind their island's ruin (below). The ledger is the only writer of rubbings and gold: the room calls its operations and never moves either itself, and after every world tick it checks `checkLedger` and its own invariant (every player the ledger counts in the match has a ship, and every ship such a player) in development and tests.
- **Collecting and claiming.** Holding E moored at a dock is one gesture: E moors, and the same hold works on E's target there, the island's first sealed source of a type the player lacks, else a cached rubbing of a type they lack (fixed type order). The room continues the ledger's hold every held tick; releasing E, casting off, a reservation or a disconnect cancels it, and progress resets. Starting a hold ends protection on the next tick.
- **Settlement order.** Each world tick: `advanceLedger` (a closed choice window settles with the default); the §12 timers (duel absence, seat expiry into a cache at the respawn dock); `stepEncounters`, whose reports tell the ledger a fight's result and the rules its end, and tell the rules `settled` only once the ledger has settled the duel; then the holds. On a win with an eligible type the winner gets 5 s to send `choose-theft`; a draw, a cancellation or a win with nothing to take settles at once (gold still moves on a win). Only then do the players return. The fighters' lobby stays in their views through the choice. Both fighters' notices carry the settlement's tick, who picked the stolen type (`settledChoice`: the winner, or the default at the deadline) and the choice's deadline tick, so the purse says "You chose Moon" (the loser: "They chose Moon") or "Taken by default: Moon". The web client maps a key (1, 2) or a click on option *n* to a type in one pure function (`chosenTheftType`, `hud.ts`) before it sends `choose-theft`.
- **Messages.** `choose-theft` `{ duel, type }` (protocol v6): the opaque key of the sender's own duel lobby and a rubbing type, zod-validated, at most 64 bytes and 8 a second; the ledger accepts it only from the winner, inside the window, for an eligible type, and otherwise changes nothing. Collecting and claiming need no message: E is the input's interact button.
- **What each client sees (§16).** Gold, rubbings, the hold and its progress, the last results and the theft options are in the player's own `status` entry only. The island's sealed types and a cache's contents are filled in only while the player is moored at that island's dock or that cache's dock. A cache is a contentless marker at its dock, in a view within the sight radius. Integration tests check raw frames: an onlooker in sight of a collection and a duel never receives a rubbing type at all.
- **Leaving.** A reservation that expires removes the player and puts their remaining rubbings in one cache at the dock the encounter rules would respawn them at; a quit (or Colyseus' outer bound) forfeits a duel in progress and caches the rest at the dock nearest the ship by sea (`seaPathCosts`). No path removes a ship while the ledger still counts its player. A cache never despawns; claimed empty, it disappears.

## The match: lobby to results (§2, §5, `match-online`)

- **Lobby.** A private match opens in its lobby (`phase` in the synced state). Its players are listed by seat ("Player 2": join order from 1; the state names players by seat, never by session id, so a ship's id still first reaches a client when it comes into sight, §16). The first joiner hosts (the host passes on when they leave). The host's `start-match` (zod-validated, empty, 4 a second) goes to the match module's `stepMatch`, which starts the ready countdown with 2 or more players present (`PRIVATE_MIN_PLAYERS`, the single source: the content's `privateMatch.minPlayers` of 1 is stale and not read) and otherwise answers `start-refused` (`too-few`, `not-host`). From the countdown on, the listing's metadata says `started` and admission refuses every join with "That match has already started" (the room's `onJoin` refuses too); if the countdown falls back to the lobby (fewer than 2 left), joins reopen. Ships are held (neutral input) until control starts and again after the end.
- **Ready and departure.** The countdown lasts `readyTicks` (20 s) while clients preload (the arena scene is already in the page's one game). The flow's `control-started` tick starts everything that counts from it: the encounter rules' state with every ship protected for `spawnProtectionTicks` (45 s, which is also the departure's length), the claim config (`createClaimConfig`, its `deadlineTick` = control start + `deadlineTicks`), and the intel config and state. The timer the HUD shows is the match module's `remaining`, whose duration is the claim rules' `deadlineTicks`: both configs are built from one set of rules (`matchConfigFor`, `claimConfigFor` in `matchFlow.ts`), and a unit test and an integration test hold them equal.
- **Tick order** (each world tick while the match runs): `advanceLedger` (closed theft windows), the §12 timers, then §5's order: **encounters** (accepted reservations first) → the ledger's holds → **claim** channel (`stepClaim`: every ship with `holdsAllTypes` from the ledger, E, speed, connection, protection, and the encounter rules' reserved duels) → **match flow** (`stepMatch`: the joins, leaves and starts since the last tick, this tick's accomplishments, and the claim's `match-ended`) → **intel reveals** (`stepIntel`). Before control start only the timers and the flow run. The room drops reports naming a player the flow does not know before calling `stepMatch`, which throws on them: one pure function over plain data (`knownFlowReports`, `apps/server/src/flowReports.ts`) drops a duel's end naming an unknown fighter, a claim's end naming an unknown winner and any accomplishment naming an unknown player, and keeps joins (known from then on), leaves, starts and a fault. The room handles no `join-refused`: it reports a join only in the lobby (its `onJoin` refuses one after it), a lobby step applies joins before any start, and the room seats no more players than the flow has seats.
- **Reveals.** The intel module reads the ledger's rubbings and the ships each tick; the room delivers only its reveal messages (rumors and the journal come with `intel-online`), each to exactly its recipients as `reveal` messages: `final-sector` to everyone at the first full set (also kept in the public state, name and index only), `final-route` with the exact claim point only to a full-set holder (also in that player's own status, with `routeActive`), `final-route-inactive` to a holder who lost a type, `sector-reveal` at minute 20 and `carrier-report` from minute 28 to everyone. An integration test checks raw frames: the other player never receives a `final-route`. The browser shows each as a banner and in a list; the holder gets a compass line, an arrow off the ship, the treasure circle and a minimap mark. In play everyone else's compass shows, inactive, "No treasure route yet". The page's decisions are pure view models, unit-tested branch by branch: `flowView` (`flowHud.ts`: each flow element's text, state and visibility) and `treasureView` (`treasureView.ts`: the sea scene's circle, marks, arrow and claim rings as shapes); `applyFlow` and the scene's `drawTreasure` only copy them into the page and the canvas.
- **The claim.** Stopped inside the treasure circle, holding every type and E, unreserved: the claim module's channel runs for `channelTicks` (10 s); starting it ends protection (the encounter rules hear it on the next tick). The player's status carries the channel's progress and the last reset's reason (moved, released, a duel, a lost type, a disconnect); the claim panel shows them with "Any rival in range can interrupt you with a grapple". The room can't produce a lost-type reset (`ineligible`) in a running channel: a player loses a type only through a duel's theft, and that duel's reservation resets the channel (`duel`) on the tick it's accepted, long before the settlement moves the rubbing. The claim module's own tests cover that branch, and the claim panel's unit test shows its text. Ships channelling show it to whoever sees them (a gold ring), and those players are warned. On `match-ended` the flow ends the match: outcomes freeze (a running duel is cancelled without theft, no ship takes input, nothing more is stepped).
- **Endings and results.** `claim` (a winner), `deadline` (no winner; a claim completing on the deadline tick wins), `abandoned` (everyone left after the lobby; stepped once more as the room closes) and `aborted` (a world tick that throws is caught as §12's server fault). The accomplishments come from the ledger (`docs/objectives.md`) and settled duels: a rubbing leaving a source is collected, one leaving a cache is a cache claimed, one moving between players is a theft and a loss, one going into a cache is a loss; a settled win or draw counts for both fighters, a cancelled duel for neither. The results (the flow's) are synced to everyone once, shown until players leave (Back to lobby returns to the landing page), and recorded in the process's outcome list (`recordedOutcomes`).
- **Seeds.** One private master secret per match (32 bytes of `node:crypto`'s `randomBytes`). Each system's seed is `HMAC-SHA-256(secret, "pirate-sea-race/seed/v1/" + system)`, its first four bytes: `world`, `ledger`, `final-socket`, `intel`, `ruins`, `fruit` (the fruit deal), and each duel's `duel:<n>`. No raw seed feeds two systems and none reads the match code; unit and integration tests check both.
- **Test hooks** (`MatchTuning.testHooks`, off by default, never set by an entry point): `injectFault()` makes the next world tick throw (an `aborted` ending), `pauseAfterTick(tick)` / `resumeWorld()` stop the clock after a tick so a test lines an input up with an exact tick (a grapple landing on a claim's completion tick, a claim completing on the deadline tick), and `injectFlowReports(reports)` adds reports to the flow's next step (a ghost player's, to show they are dropped).
- **Coverage.** `docs/match-online-coverage.md` lists every room-level and UI branch this feature added or changed, each with the test that fails without it. `recordedOutcomes` keeps only the latest 64 (`outcomes.ts`).

## Ruins in the room (§3, §11, §16, `ruins-online`)

- **Dealing.** `createMatchRuins` (`apps/server/src/ruins.ts`) deals `docs/ruins.md`'s ruins once per match from the `ruins` seed (never the ledger's, so no clue reveals the deal). Sources start locked. The first solve's `sources-unlocked` calls `unlockSource` for each of the island's sources. Every solver's `gold-awarded` calls `grantGold` (reason `ruin`, key the island), which pays 40 once per player per ruin.
- **Presence and messages** (protocol v8). Each world tick in play, after the encounters, the room reports every player's presence to the rules: the island they're moored at (if connected and in the world) and whether a duel holds them. A leave reports at once. So casting off, a duel or a disconnect closes the session by the next tick. `open-ruin` (R) sends `ruin-clue` back to the sender only, strictly parsed. `answer-ruin` `{ requestId, attempt }` is judged once per request id (the last 16 are remembered, and a retry gets the first verdict). `ruin-result` carries only the outcome, the refusal, the lockout tick, the gold paid and whether this solve unlocked the island. Both are zod-validated, 8 a second, and read only in play.
- **Visibility.** The player's own `status` carries the ruin's state where they're moored, their session and their lockout. The `ruins` map's per-island markers (`unlocked`) are in a view only when the island is within sight or the player is moored there. The answer never leaves the server; an integration test checks raw frames.
- **Browser.** `ruinPanel.ts` holds pure view models and entry logic, plus the `RuinPanel` controller that `main.ts` feeds. While it's open, the helm is neutral.
- **Test-only** `testRuins` (env `PIRATE_SEA_RACE_TEST_RUINS`, or the next-match route): `open` unlocks an island at the start. `sequence` or `navigation` pins its kind, using the first derived `ruins:<n>` seed that deals it. Integration tuning and the browser server open every island unless a test asks otherwise. The branch table is `docs/ruins-online-coverage.md`.

## Fruits in the room (§9, §16, `fruit-kits-online`)

- **Pedestals and the deal.** `pedestalSites` (`apps/server/src/fruits.ts`) puts one pedestal on each regular island at its highest-id dock (4 in the slice). `createMatchFruits` deals `docs/fruits.md`'s fruit onto them from the `fruit` seed. Test-only `testFruits` (env `PIRATE_SEA_RACE_TEST_FRUITS`, for example `ember,smoke,smoke,ember`) pins the kit on each island's pedestal. The browser server pins that deal.
- **Eating** (protocol v9). F held is the input's fruit button (`Buttons.Fruit`). Each world tick in play, after the encounters and the ruins' presence and before the ledger's holds and the claim, the room calls `stepFruits` with every player's facts: the pedestal at the dock they're moored at (none while waiting to respawn), F, whether a duel reserves them, and whether they're disconnected (a drop cancels the channel as `disconnected`). Each player's last result (`eaten:<kit>`, `interrupted:<reason>`, `refused:<reason>`) and progress go into their own `status` with their `kit`. A refusal at the pedestal they just emptied doesn't replace the meal.
- **Inspecting.** `inspect-fruit` (`{}`, 8 a second, in play, not in a duel) sends `fruit-kit` to the sender only: the island, and the kit with its §9 description, or `full: false`. Both are zod-validated and strict.
- **Visibility.** `pedestals` markers (island, dock, place, `full`) are in a view when the dock is in sight. The deal never leaves the server except in an inspection. A player's kit is only in their own status until a duel. At a duel's start the lobby's `kits` (`"ember,duelist"`, the attacker's first) reaches its two fighters. Integration tests check raw frames.
- **Into duels.** `openSeaDuel` passes `kitOf` for both fighters to the `DuelMachine`, which creates the frame-0 state with them and syncs them in the lobby. Both clients build the same state from the seed and the kits, so the per-frame hashes cover them. No rule clears a meal, so the kit survives a lost duel.
- **Browser.** `fruitPanel.ts` holds the HUD's kit and pedestal lines, the panel's view model and the `FruitPanel` controller. `pageKeys.ts` routes a keydown to one panel at a time and skips keys typed into text fields. `arenaDrawing.ts` turns `fighterTells` into the arena's shapes: bolts, smoke screens, the obscured startup flash, the reappearance, and threats only for striking moves. The arena reports `data-bolts`, `data-zones` and `data-tells`. The branch table is `docs/fruit-kits-online-coverage.md`.

## The duel (combat spike)

- **Duel room.** `DuelRoom` (room name `duel`) holds one duel, a `DuelMachine`: two players, or one in practice against a server-side dummy (player two, `idle` or `guard`). It is admitted like a match, by the same code in `admission.ts`: a one-time create token, `onAuth` before any seat, the room's own check, `filterBy(['code', 'createToken'])`, no token in the listing. The countdown (180 frames) starts once every seat is taken; the machine probes round trips during it, chooses the shared input delay 30 frames before the end, then steps `DuelAuthority` at 60 Hz, which the room's `setFixedTimestep` drives. Inputs go through `DuelInputGate`, which admits them through the same `InputAdmission` as the world's `InputGate` (the rate window and the protocol validation: 128 bytes, 60 a second of room ticks, increasing sequence, 30 frames of lead), so the two cannot drift, and counts its drops. Frame bundles and probes are Colyseus messages; the lobby is a small Schema state. A drop keeps the seat for 10 s (`allowReconnection`); leaving, or staying away, forfeits, decided at the next frame boundary (two forfeits on one frame: no winner). The rules and rates are in `docs/duel.md`.
- **One rollback core.** The browser's `DuelClient` and `HeadlessDuelClient` both run `DuelClientSession` from `@pirate-sea-race/simulation/netcode`; they differ only in transport and input (keyboard or script), and each plays over a duel room or a match room. The arena draws the predicted state; the HUD shows the confirmed one (server-equal health, stamina and clock) and the room's result. `window.__duel` exposes the session's counters and tagged inputs, read-only, for the browser tests.
- **Impairment harness.** `ImpairmentProxy` is a TCP proxy (Node's `net`, no new dependency) between a client and the server. It forwards HTTP untouched in content and splits the WebSocket stream into frames; each frame waits half the round trip plus a uniform ±jitter/2 in its direction, never overtaking the frame before it, and a lost frame (seeded draw) waits a further retransmission timeout (200 ms), stalling everything behind it as TCP does. `sever()` cuts every connection (optionally refusing new ones) for the reconnect tests. `tests/integration/duelHarness.test.ts` runs a scripted duel between two headless clients through it, with no impairment and at 80 ms, 20 ms jitter and 1 % loss (and `seaDuelHarness.test.ts` the same duel at sea, at 80 ms, 20 ms and 1 %, with the scripts and budget of `harness.ts`), and requires no desync at any of the ~180 hash checks per client, no rate-limited input, and corrections at most one per change of the opponent's applied input plus one per own substituted input, and at most 8 a second; it prints and annotates the counts. `replayRecordedDuel` replays a log (for example the pairs a client received) with `replayDuel`.
- **Dev latency.** Only in `npm run dev` (`import.meta.env.DEV`), `?rtt=80&jitter=20` on the page delays that browser's duel socket both ways, probes and pings included; the build smoke test checks the production bundle does not contain it. The browser checks run the production build, so the setting is tested below the browser: `apps/web/src/devLatency.ts` has no DOM dependency, unit tests with fake timers check its delay, jitter bound and order on a real SDK room, and `tests/integration/devLatency.test.ts` wraps two headless duel clients in it and checks that the room's measured round trip and chosen input delay rise above the same duel without it.

## Rules the code keeps

- **Purity.** `simulation`, `protocol` and `content` import no Phaser, Colyseus, DOM, timers, wall-clock time or `Math.random`, and call no floating-point transcendental `Math` function. Their tsconfig leaves out the DOM library, and `tests/unit/purity.test.ts` fails on a violation.
- **Integers.** Every number in the simulation state is an integer, so `hashState` (64-bit FNV-1a over a canonical serialization) does not depend on the JavaScript engine; a determinism test replays an input log.
- **One clock.** The room steps the simulation 60 times a second with Colyseus `setFixedTimestep`. World logic runs on frames divisible by 3 (20 Hz); the room then mirrors the plain state into its Schema and updates the views, and Colyseus patches clients at 20 Hz. Integration tests measure both rates, also with eight sailing ships in one cluster.
- **The server alone writes state.** At sea, clients send only `input` messages, `{seq, frame, buttons, moveX, moveY}`, validated with zod (the grapple is a button: the rules choose its target, never the client). `InputGate` drops, and counts, messages over the rate cap (60 per second of match time) or over 128 bytes, malformed ones (axes outside [-1, 1] are rejected, not clamped), ones whose sequence number is not higher than the last, and ones tagged more than 30 frames ahead. A held input lapses to neutral after 15 frames. An accepted world input applies from the server's next step whatever frame it names, since sea clients do not predict; a duel input applies to exactly the frame it names (`docs/duel.md`). Unknown message types are dropped. Colyseus's own limits sit above these: WebSocket frames over 4 KiB and more than 240 messages a second disconnect.
- **Joining.** Matches and duels share the admission code (`apps/server/src/admission.ts`). Colyseus serves `create`, `join`, `joinOrCreate` and `joinById` over HTTP and reserves a seat before any room check, so a private match is guarded in three layers. The static `onAuth` runs before any seat is reserved: it refuses a mismatched protocol version (426), a request with neither or both of `code` and `createToken` or a malformed token (400), an unknown code (404) and a full match (409). A `create` carries a one-time 128-bit `createToken`; the room is registered with `filterBy(['code', 'createToken'])` and `onCreate` replaces the listing's metadata with `{code, custom}`, so no listing holds a token and a token-carrying request can only create. The room's `onJoin` is the backstop, and the only check `joinById` meets after `onAuth`: one seat with the creator's token, then only seats with the match's code (404 for another code, 403 otherwise). Refusal messages stay under 100 bytes. A caller who knows a room id can still hold seats with `joinById` until each reservation expires (15 s).
- **Rendering.** The client draws the ships the server sent 100 ms in the past, interpolating between patches; the HUD lists their latest decoded state. The camera follows the player's ship over a Phaser tile map at 24 px a tile (the 480 px sight circle fits the 800 × 560 view) that leaves open sea to the background colour, keeping a software renderer fast. The sea does not predict; the duel arena does (above). Both of the page's Phaser games use the canvas renderer: the standalone duel page's arena, and the match page's one game holding the sea and the arena. With `Phaser.AUTO`, headless Chromium (the GPU-less case: WebGL in software, on the main thread) starved the duel client's 4 ms tick during a fight at sea: the `sea-duel` browser test, which records the `DuelClient`'s tick intervals through the fight and requires their 95th percentile under 16 ms, measured 135 ms. With `Phaser.CANVAS` it measured 8.5 ms (host) and 8.9 ms (guest), so the match game now uses the canvas renderer too.

## Toolchain

npm workspaces, TypeScript 7.0.2 (`tsc` for typechecks and package builds), Vite 8.3.0 (web build), Vitest 5.0.1 (`unit` and `integration` projects), tsx (map script and dev server), Phaser 4.2.1, `colyseus` 0.18.8 with `@colyseus/schema` 5.0.34, `@colyseus/sdk` 0.18.4, zod 4.6.5, Playwright 1.63.0. Workspace packages export a `@pirate-sea-race/source` condition that points at `src/`, so development and tests need no build. `npm run build` compiles each package to `dist/` in dependency order, then `scripts/smoke-build.ts` loads every workspace export from `dist/`, starts the built server on a free port, creates a match through the SDK, waits for the creator's ship and checks that no test-placement route answers, with every wait bounded. `colyseus` brings `uWebSockets.js` in from GitHub, so `npm ci` needs github.com as well as the npm registry. The duel added no dependency: `packages/test-tools` now also depends on the workspace's `@pirate-sea-race/simulation`, and the smoke test also loads `@pirate-sea-race/simulation/netcode` from `dist/`, checks the web bundle for the dev-only latency setting, and plays the first frames of a practice duel on the built server.

An island's rubbings are locked behind its ruin: moored there, press R to read its clue and answer it (+40 gold; the first solver opens the island for everyone). Some docks have a fruit pedestal: press F to read its fruit, then hold F for three seconds to eat it (its kit replaces your specials in duels). Then keep holding E to collect its rubbing (six seconds), or to claim one from a recovery cache there. J: grapple the nearest ship ahead within six tiles; it lands after a second, unless the target sails out of range or out of its aim. A grapple that lands starts a duel; its winner has five seconds to pick a rubbing to steal (1 or 2). Hold every rubbing type and your compass points to the final island: stop inside its treasure circle and hold E for ten seconds to win.

          Status

          Move: WASD or the arrow keys (hold back to guard, down-back for lows). J light, K heavy, U and I specials, Shift dash, J and K together to throw (or to escape a throw). Down + K sweeps low, forward + K launches, down + J is the anti-air.

          import { Buttons } from "@pirate-sea-race/protocol"; /** What the player asks of their ship: protocol axes (moveX turns, moveY is the throttle, up ahead) and buttons. */ export interface Helm { readonly moveX: number; readonly moveY: number; readonly buttons: number; } export const NEUTRAL_HELM: Helm = { moveX: 0, moveY: 0, buttons: 0 }; const KEYS = { left: ["KeyA", "ArrowLeft"], right: ["KeyD", "ArrowRight"], up: ["KeyW", "ArrowUp"], down: ["KeyS", "ArrowDown"], interact: ["KeyE"], grapple: ["KeyJ"], } as const; /** Buttons kept from a tap until the next read: interact (E) and the grapple (J, §8). */ const LATCHED: readonly [readonly string[], number][] = [ [KEYS.interact, Buttons.Interact], [KEYS.grapple, Buttons.Grapple], ]; const HELM_CODES = new Set(Object.values(KEYS).flat()); /** Converts two opposing keys into one axis: both held is neutral, whatever order they were pressed in (§8). */ export function axis(negative: boolean, positive: boolean): number { return (positive ? 1 : 0) - (negative ? 1 : 0); } /** * The keyboard input adapter (§8 defaults): up is throttle, down brakes (and reverses slowly from a stop), left and * right turn, E interacts (docks), J grapples. It tracks held keys and releases them all (and forgets a tap) when the * window loses focus, so a ship never keeps sailing, docks or grapples on a key the page missed. The page reads it on * a timer, so a tap of E or J that goes down and up between two reads is kept until the next read, as the duel * keyboard keeps its taps: it counts once. */ export class KeyboardHelm { private readonly held = new Set(); private tapped = 0; constructor(target: Window) { target.addEventListener("keydown", (event) => { if (!HELM_CODES.has(event.code) || isTyping(event.target)) return; event.preventDefault(); this.press(event.code); }); target.addEventListener("keyup", (event) => this.release(event.code)); target.addEventListener("blur", () => { this.held.clear(); this.tapped = 0; }); } press(code: string): void { if (!HELM_CODES.has(code)) return; this.held.add(code); for (const [codes, button] of LATCHED) if (codes.includes(code)) this.tapped |= button; } release(code: string): void { this.held.delete(code); } /** What is held now, plus a button tapped since the last read. Reading it clears the tap. */ helm(): Helm { const any = (codes: readonly string[]) => codes.some((code) => this.held.has(code)); let buttons = this.tapped; for (const [codes, button] of LATCHED) if (any(codes)) buttons |= button; this.tapped = 0; return { moveX: axis(any(KEYS.left), any(KEYS.right)), moveY: axis(any(KEYS.up), any(KEYS.down)), buttons, }; } } /** * Whether a key went to a text field (an input or a text area), which keeps its keys: the helm and the page's panels * ignore them. Read from the element's tag, so unit tests in Node can pass a stand-in. */ export function isTyping(target: EventTarget | null): boolean { const tag = (target as { tagName?: unknown } | null)?.tagName; return tag === "INPUT" || tag === "TEXTAREA"; }

          import { Buttons } from "@pirate-sea-race/protocol"; /** What the player asks of their ship: protocol axes (moveX turns, moveY is the throttle, up ahead) and buttons. */ export interface Helm { readonly moveX: number; readonly moveY: number; readonly buttons: number; } export const NEUTRAL_HELM: Helm = { moveX: 0, moveY: 0, buttons: 0 }; const KEYS = { left: ["KeyA", "ArrowLeft"], right: ["KeyD", "ArrowRight"], up: ["KeyW", "ArrowUp"], down: ["KeyS", "ArrowDown"], interact: ["KeyE"], grapple: ["KeyJ"], } as const; /** Buttons kept from a tap until the next read: interact (E) and the grapple (J, §8). */ const LATCHED: readonly [readonly string[], number][] = [ [KEYS.interact, Buttons.Interact], [KEYS.grapple, Buttons.Grapple], ]; const HELM_CODES = new Set(Object.values(KEYS).flat()); /** Converts two opposing keys into one axis: both held is neutral, whatever order they were pressed in (§8). */ export function axis(negative: boolean, positive: boolean): number { return (positive ? 1 : 0) - (negative ? 1 : 0); } /** * The keyboard input adapter (§8 defaults): up is throttle, down brakes (and reverses slowly from a stop), left and * right turn, E interacts (docks), J grapples. It tracks held keys and releases them all (and forgets a tap) when the * window loses focus, so a ship never keeps sailing, docks or grapples on a key the page missed. The page reads it on * a timer, so a tap of E or J that goes down and up between two reads is kept until the next read, as the duel * keyboard keeps its taps: it counts once. */ export class KeyboardHelm { private readonly held = new Set(); private tapped = 0; constructor(target: Window) { target.addEventListener("keydown", (event) => { if (!HELM_CODES.has(event.code) || isTyping(event.target)) return; event.preventDefault(); this.press(event.code); }); target.addEventListener("keyup", (event) => this.release(event.code)); target.addEventListener("blur", () => { this.held.clear(); this.tapped = 0; }); } press(code: string): void { if (!HELM_CODES.has(code)) return; this.held.add(code); for (const [codes, button] of LATCHED) if (codes.includes(code)) this.tapped |= button; } release(code: string): void { this.held.delete(code); } /** What is held now, plus a button tapped since the last read. Reading it clears the tap. */ helm(): Helm { const any = (codes: readonly string[]) => codes.some((code) => this.held.has(code)); let buttons = this.tapped; for (const [codes, button] of LATCHED) if (any(codes)) buttons |= button; this.tapped = 0; return { moveX: axis(any(KEYS.left), any(KEYS.right)), moveY: axis(any(KEYS.up), any(KEYS.down)), buttons, }; } } /** * Whether a key went to a text field (an input or a text area), which keeps its keys: the helm and the page's panels * ignore them. Only then does it call `purchase` with the client's request id. On `ok && !replayed` it asks intel to deliver the rumor under that (player, request id). On `ok && replayed` it resends the rumor already delivered. On `!ok` (`replayed` or not) it sends the refusal and delivers nothing: a `replayed` refusal is the original answer, so a delayed retry never buys what the player was refused. A request whose (player, client request id) the room already decided is answered from the room's own record first (a bought id resends its lead, a refused id the same refusal; it keeps every bought id and each player's last 16 refusals). Otherwise the request waits for a world tick (a pending id's retry is merged, and a third waiting request is refused `busy`). Each tick the room takes at most one request per player, in the reveal step, after every other ledger operation of the tick. It checks, in order, that the buyer's ship is moored at a dock on this tick, the ledger's state (connected, out of any duel, at least the rumor's price, read with `findPlayer`, `activeDuelOf` and `itemPrice`) and intel's `targetedRumorAvailability`; a failure is a refusal the room records, and the ledger never sees it. Then it runs `stepIntel` with the request under a room-namespaced id (`<player>:<client id>`), and only when the outcome is `rumor` or `sighting` does it call `purchase` with the client's id. Nothing moves that player's gold between the check and the charge, so a refused `purchase` there is a broken invariant: the world tick throws and the match faults (§12). Every other outcome is one recorded refusal with intel's reason, uncharged. The ledger's own replay of a purchase id is therefore never reached by the room. `economy-online`'s dockside shop will list the same purchase.'''

s=s.replace(a,b)
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

lines: - **`purchase({ requestId, playerId, item, tick })`** buys a `rumor` (25) or a `tonic` (30). The gold goes to `goldSpent`, not to another player. Request ids are **per player**: outcomes are kept in `requests` under (player, request id), so another player's id never refuses or reveals yours. The refusals `insufficient-gold`, `tonic-limit` (a third tonic), `player-in-duel` (fighting or in the choice window) and `player-disconnected` are decisions: they are kept, charge nothing, and change only `requests` and `tick`. Malformed, stale, `unknown-player` and `player-left` requests are not kept and return the same state. Repeating a kept (player, request id) with the same item returns the original outcome, a purchase (`ok: true`) or a refusal (`ok: false`, with `refusal`), with `replayed: true` and the same state, whatever its tick and even if it would succeed now: a retry never pays twice and never buys what was refused. The same id for the other item is a `duplicate`. A player keeps at most 16 refusals; the 17th evicts their oldest, and an evicted id is decided afresh if retried. Purchases are never evicted.

- **`useTonic({ playerId, tick, atSea, grappled })`** spends one tonic and makes it active on ticks `tick` to `tick + 239`: `activeTonic(state, playerId, t)` is true from `startTick` and false from `endTick` = `startTick + 240`. It is refused with `tonic-active`, `no-tonic`, `not-at-sea`, `grappled` (a flag the caller sets from the world), `player-in-duel` or `player-disconnected`. A lost duel keeps the tonics; leaving drops them and ends an active one. The ledger never touches movement: the sailing code reads `activeTonic` and adds its +10 %.
- **The invariant** becomes balances + `goldSpent` = `goldIssued`, with `goldIssued` = purses + grants.

-- **Rumor flow:** the room first asks the intel module whether a targeted rumor is available for the player (a missing type with a lead). Only then does it call `purchase` with the client's request id. On `ok && !replayed` it asks intel to deliver the rumor under that (player, request id). On `ok && replayed` it resends the rumor already delivered. On `!ok` (`replayed` or not) it sends the refusal and delivers nothing: a `replayed` refusal is the original answer, so a delayed retry never buys what the player was refused. A rumor that cannot be delivered is never bought.

+- **Rumor flow** (`intel-online`, `docs/architecture.md`): the ledger has no refunds, so the room charges only for a lead intel has delivered. A request whose (player, client request id) the room already decided is answered from the room's own record first (a bought id resends its lead, a refused id the same refusal; it keeps every bought id and each player's last 16 refusals). Otherwise the request waits for a world tick (a pending id's retry is merged, and a third waiting request is refused `busy`). Each tick the room takes at most one request per player, in the reveal step, after every other ledger operation of the tick. It checks, in order, that the buyer's ship is moored at a dock on this tick, the ledger's state (connected, out of any duel, at least the rumor's price, read with `findPlayer`, `activeDuelOf` and `itemPrice`) and intel's `targetedRumorAvailability`; a failure is a refusal the room records, and the ledger never sees it. Then it runs `stepIntel` with the request under a room-namespaced id (`<player>:<client id>`), and only when the outcome is `rumor` or `sighting` does it call `purchase` with the client's id. Nothing moves that player's gold between the check and the charge, so a refused `purchase` there is a broken invariant: the world tick throws and the match faults (§12). Every other outcome is one recorded refusal with intel's reason, uncharged. The ledger's own replay of a purchase id is therefore never reached by the room. `economy-online`'s dockside shop will list the same purchase.
